what_it_does: When a program multiplies a sparse matrix (a grid of numbers where most entries are zero) by a vector, the best way to do it depends heavily on how many zeros there are and how they are arranged — and different processor architectures prefer different strategies. Existing math libraries pick one fixed algorithm and stick with it, missing easy performance gains. This paper presents SSpMV, a system that uses a multi-modal neural network (a learned model that fuses several different descriptions of the matrix's structure and density) to predict which algorithm and settings will run fastest for a given matrix on a given chip. The multimodal component, called MM-Adapter, combines pattern-based, density-based, and structural descriptions of the matrix to give the predictor richer information than any single view alone. The key novelty is treating algorithm selection as a learning problem informed by multiple complementary representations of the input, rather than relying on hand-written rules.
